meaning: Involution — extreme competition where everyone works harder but no one gets ahead. Like a rat race with no winner.
origin: Academic term gone viral ~2020. Students studying 20hrs/day to outcompete each other, but grades stay the same.
example: 现在大家都在内卷，连周末也要学习。(Xiànzài dàjiā dōu zài nèi juǎn, lián zhōumò yě yào xuéxí.) — Everyone is in the rat race now, even studying on weekends.
usage: Casual / very common online and in conversation

meaning: Lying flat — choosing to do the bare minimum, rejecting hustle culture. The opposite of 内卷.
origin: Went viral in 2021. Young Chinese rejecting societal pressure to work, marry, buy houses.
example: 我决定躺平了，不想再卷了。(Wǒ juédìng tǎng píng le, bù xiǎng zài juǎn le.) — I've decided to lie flat, I don't want to compete anymore.
usage: Casual / internet slang / relatable to young people

meaning: Absolutely amazing! / So incredibly [adjective]! Can mean both 'incredible' (positive) and 'incredibly bad' depending on context.
origin: Chinese internet slang ~2021. Short form of 绝了 (jué le) with 子 suffix for cute effect.
example: 这个歌手唱得绝绝子！(Zhège gēshǒu chàng de jué jué zi!) — This singer is absolutely incredible!
usage: Internet only / used by Gen Z / not formal at all

meaning: Wage worker / working person. Used humorously and self-deprecatingly about being a salaried employee grinding every day.
origin: Went viral after a video of a worker saying '打工人，打工魂' (worker soul). Became a badge of honor.
example: 又到周一了，打工人继续上班。(Yòu dào zhōuyī le, dǎgōngrén jìxù shàngbān.) — Monday again, time for us workers to grind.

meaning: To slack off, goof off, or secretly do personal things while at work. Literally 'touching fish'.
origin: From the saying 'muddy waters make it easier to catch fish' — hard to be caught slacking when it's chaotic.
example: 老板不在，大家都在摸鱼。(Lǎobǎn bù zài, dàjiā dōu zài mō yú.) — The boss is away, everyone is slacking off.

meaning: GOAT / Greatest of all time. Abbreviation of 永远的神 (yǒngyuǎn de shén = eternal god/legend).
origin: Chinese gaming/esports community. Used when praising a player or celebrity who is on another level.
example: 这个球员真的yyds！(Zhège qiúyuán zhēn de yyds!) — This player is literally the GOAT!
usage: Internet only / texting / do NOT say out loud — just type the letters

meaning: My defenses are broken / I'm emotionally moved. Used when something hits you deeply — can be sad, touching, or overwhelmingly cute.
origin: Gaming term (defense broken) adapted for emotional context. Went mainstream ~2021.
example: 看了这个视频我破防了，太感动了。(Kàn le zhège shìpín wǒ pò fáng le, tài gǎndòng le.) — I watched this video and broke down, I'm so moved.
usage: Very common online / casual / emotional contexts

meaning: Buddhist-style / chill / laid-back. Describing someone who doesn't get worked up, is indifferent to competition, and goes with the flow.
origin: Japanese term adapted in China ~2017. Buddhist monks don't chase material things — the attitude.
example: 他很佛系，什么都无所谓。(Tā hěn fó xì, shénme dōu wú suǒwèi.) — He's very chill, nothing bothers him.
usage: Casual / positive connotation / common in conversation

meaning: Awesome / impressive / so cool! Used to praise someone's skills. Like saying 'nice!' or 'respect!'
origin: Gaming slang — 溜 (liū) means smooth/skilled, 666 sounds like 溜溜溜 = super smooth. Now used everywhere.
example: 你一口气做了100个俯卧撑？666！(Nǐ yīkǒuqì zuòle 100 gè fǔwòchēng? 666!) — You did 100 push-ups in one go? Respect!
usage: Very common / works in text and speech / all ages

meaning: The ultimate overachiever / the person who works hardest in the 内卷 (rat race). Both admired and gently mocked.
origin: Combines 内卷 + 王 (king). The person who out-hustles everyone.
example: 他每天学到凌晨两点，真是卷王。(Tā měitiān xué dào língchén liǎng diǎn, zhēnshi juǎn wáng.) — He studies until 2am every night, true grind king.
usage: Casual / can be compliment or teasing

meaning: Lemon spirit / jealous person. Someone who is obviously jealous but pretends not to be. Like being sour.
origin: Internet slang — lemons are sour, 精 means spirit/essence. A jealous person is 'lemon essence'.
example: 她一直说别人男友不好，其实她是柠檬精。(Tā yīzhí shuō biérén nán yǒu bù hǎo, qíshí tā shì níng méng jīng.) — She keeps saying others' boyfriends are bad, she's just jealous.
usage: Light teasing / friendly humor / common online

meaning: Humble-bragging / showing off wealth or success while pretending to complain. 'Versailles style' — named after the palace.
origin: From a Japanese manga about Versailles life. A Chinese blogger used it to describe people who brag by fake-complaining.
example: 他说'我开奔驰好累啊'，这人太凡尔赛了。(Tā shuō 'Wǒ kāi Bēnchí hǎo lèi a', zhè rén tài fán ěr sài le.) — He said 'driving my Mercedes is so tiring', what a humble-bragger.
usage: Common / funny / used to call out braggarts

meaning: To fix/clean up the workplace. Gen Z attitude of not tolerating unfair work culture, setting boundaries with bosses.
origin: Went viral in 2022 when young workers started pushing back on overtime culture and unreasonable demands.
example: 新来的实习生拒绝加班，说要整顿职场。(Xīn lái de shíxíshēng jùjué jiābān, shuō yào zhěng dùn zhíchǎng.) — The new intern refused overtime, saying they're fixing work culture.
usage: Trending / Gen Z attitude / conversation and social media

meaning: Social anxiety / socially awkward. Short for 社交恐惧症 (social phobia). Used casually to describe being introverted.
origin: Shortened from the medical term, now used casually by anyone who feels awkward in social situations.
example: 我有点社恐，不太喜欢聚会。(Wǒ yǒudiǎn shè kǒng, bù tài xǐhuān jùhuì.) — I have a bit of social anxiety, I don't really like parties.

meaning: Heart moved / feeling a flutter / getting a crush feeling. That butterflies-in-stomach feeling when you like someone.
origin: Classic Chinese — 心 (heart) + 动 (moved). Not new slang but widely used in romantic contexts and reality TV show names.
example: 看到他我就心动了。(Kàn dào tā wǒ jiù xīn dòng le.) — My heart fluttered when I saw him.
usage: Romantic contexts / everyday speech / not slang, but widely used
